en: The Sūtra of the Questions of Śrīgupta (also titled *The Path of the Bodhisattva*), translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
He was accompanied by a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
At that time, there was a son of a householder named Śikhaṇḍin, who, together with five hundred disciples, set out from the great kingdom of Rājagṛha, intending to go to the Bamboo Grove.
Before they had arrived, they saw from afar the Buddha walking in meditation; his physical radiance and its countless transformations were such as could not be heard of or seen by worldly people.
The five hundred disciples spoke among themselves in praise, saying:
"The Buddha’s countenance is peerlessly handsome, and his majestic spiritual power is truly such as this."
By what causes and conditions does this exist in the world?
What practices must be performed and what merits accumulated to obtain such a body?
We should go and ask him.

The five hundred disciples, with minds full of reverence, were struck with awe and solemnity; their hair stood on end as they stepped forward to prostrate before the Buddha and then withdrew to stand to one side.
Śikhaṇḍin then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha’s body is such as this, beyond what is seen in the world.
By what cause has it come to be so?”
"What were his past practices? What merits did he accumulate?
The Buddha asked Śikhaṇḍin, "What have you seen that you say, 'The Buddha’s body is such as this; it is not what can be seen in the world'?"
Śikhaṇḍin then spoke a verse before the Buddha:
“Maintaining mindfulness, he gazes upon that which cannot be seen; When the Honored One among Men walks in meditation, Lotus flowers appear beneath his feet;
His form is so upright and perfect, there is nothing lacking.”
The wisdom of the empty body can manifest the Dharma;
all lands tremble, the mounds and ruins are entirely leveled, and the high ground becomes low.
When he lifts his foot to walk in meditation, and as he has already traversed the ground, his body turns to the right upon the earth;
yet no one can perceive that the earth itself is turning.
When he lowers his feet to tread upon the earth, they vanish as soon as he walks;
yet the places where his tracks were appear as if painted.
All these marks are clearly visible, though the wheels of his marks have no color, yet they manifest themselves entirely upon the ground.
What is seen now does not exist in the world; for this reason, know him to be most venerable.
No one is able to see his crown; neither on the left nor on the right, neither in front nor behind—nowhere can he be found.
By what cause can one know their intention?
By what condition can one comprehend their wisdom?
For this reason my mind is filled with wonder; I pray that you will explain this to me in detail.
From where is this body of wisdom obtained?
What is its fundamental basis?
By what kind of dharmas is it practiced?
How shall we bring its fruit to fulfillment?
We pray that you will sever our doubts and resolve what we find perplexing.
How is the wisdom of that Buddha to be attained?
I pray that you will explain in successive order the practices that Bodhisattvas and others should perform,
by which they may personally accomplish the Mahāyāna task and attain the supernormal powers to reach the ten directions.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Vigata-mada!
What you have asked is most profound!
Most profound!
With much concern for the welfare of gods and humans, he brings them great peace and security.
Out of compassion for the ten directions and desiring to lead them to liberation, he gives rise to the mind of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and inspires all to be diligent.
The Buddha said to Sīghramati,
“I shall explain it for you.
Listen attentively!”
"Listen attentively!
Śikhaṇḍin then said,
"I accept your instruction."
The Buddha said:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who should practice six matters, they shall give rise to the seeking [of enlightenment] even before the bodhicitta has arisen.
What are these six?..."
First, dwelling in reliance upon the Buddha;
second, entering the right path and not turning back;
third, attaining internal self-awakening and clear understanding.
Fourth, one relies on oneself by virtue of having attained good spiritual friends;
fifth, one constantly maintains great vows;
sixth, one possesses no timid or weak mind and never tires of wisdom.
"These are the six.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If there is a person who relies on the Buddha-dharma, entering the right path and realizing the truths so as not to return,"
By constantly relying on spiritual friends, one thereby attains great vows.
With the inner mind fully awakened, such a person is not timid;
being completely endowed with wisdom, such a person is able to receive the Dharma.
Śikhaṇḍin addressed the Buddha, saying,
"For one who has aroused the intention, how many kinds of joy of intention are there?
The Buddha said:
"For those who have aroused the bodhicitta, there are six kinds of joyful resolve. What are the six?
First, by attaining a joyful resolve, they do not depart from the Buddha."
Second, receiving the prophecy of enlightenment and entering the Right Path;
third, acting as a sovereign physician-king to treat the birth, old age, sickness, and death of sentient beings;
fourth, acting as a general to deliver people from the five realms of existence within saṃsāra.
Fifth, I act as a great master mariner upon the ocean, delivering those swept away by the currents;
sixth, amidst the darkness, I act as a lord of great illumination, shattering ignorance.
"These are the six kinds of joy of mind.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Because they have attained the intent not to be separated from the Buddha, They receive the prophecy of their words and enter the Right Path."
Acting as a King of Physicians to heal all, one attains what is desirable through such practice.
I am the honored leader in the world, desiring to deliver all from calamities and hardships—
birth, death, old age, and sickness— and from all the attachments of humanity.
Those whom I see suffering in toil, transmigrating through the five realms of existence—
of these I shall become a great captain to ferry those in the sea across to liberation;
I shall be a great light in the darkness, giving eyes to all who are blind.
"All flattery, deceit, and folly—may all people be endowed with wisdom.
Śikhaṇḍin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"With what joyful intention [is this said], and how many merits are there for its cessation?"
The Buddha said:
“For those who have aroused the bodhicitta, there are six matters by which body and mind attain rest.
What are these six?
First, by having escaped from the diligent sufferings of hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, body and mind have attained rest;
second, by having escaped from the eight states of difficulty;
third, by having escaped from the truths [of worldly existence] and no longer entering the ninety-six types of heterodox paths.
Fourth, by attaining the various Buddha-dharmas appropriate for those who have reached the stage of liberation;
fifth, by attaining the foremost position among the vessels of the Dharma, never again to regress;
sixth, by abiding in the Buddha’s adorned teachings, never severing the path of the Buddhas.
"These are the six meritorious cessations.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"By being delivered from all evil realms, The body remains far removed from the eight states of adversity."
All those non-Buddhists who do not accept [the name of the Buddha], such as these, he completely distances himself from.
Toward the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas, and toward all people who harbor attachments, he transcends them all and gives rise to a reverent mind; he surpasses all dharmas.
I now act as a vessel for the Dharma for all, and for all Buddhas and their teachings;
furthermore, I shall not sever the Buddha’s solemn instructions, and for this reason, I have attained what is pleasing to my heart.
The substance of space may be exhausted, and echoes and reflections may also be seen;
yet for one who is not thus courageous, their practice is boundless and inexhaustible.
Viśākha addressed the Buddha, saying,
"For one who has aroused the aspiration for bodhicitta, what further dharmas should they practice and perform?
The Buddha said:
"One who has resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva should practice six things.

What are these six? First, one should practice giving; second, one should maintain the precepts; third, one should practice patience; fourth, one should practice diligence; fifth, one should practice single-minded concentration; and sixth, one should practice wisdom."
"These are the six practices.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The giver gives a great gift; If one performs these practices, one should guard the precepts."
Those who possess patience and diligence surpass those in meditation and wisdom;
having received the words of wisdom before them, they shall become heroes among men.
This merit is uniquely supreme, and it is that which all bodhisattvas ought to practice.
Thus, among all beings, his conduct is uniquely peerless;
wherever he dwells, he is a venerable hero, and those who behold him offer him countless offerings.
Viśākha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva wishes to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), by what means should they achieve it?
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva has six practices by which they swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

What are these six? First, not reckoning there is a body; second, not reckoning there is a person (*pudgala*); third, not reckoning there is a life-force (*jīva*); fourth, not reckoning there is a form (*rūpa*); fifth, not reckoning there is non-existence; sixth, not reckoning there is permanence.”
These are the six practices.
By means of these, a bodhisattva swiftly attains the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Self, person, and life-span— one should not reckon these as having form;
the mind should not conceive of existence or non-existence; the wise should keep far away from such notions.”
The causal conditions spoken of by the mouth—those causal conditions do not exist;
all phenomena have no arising, and for this reason, one attains the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
Viśākha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), by how many things does he attain all-knowledge (sarvajñatā)?”
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they attain all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) through six matters.
What are these six?

First is the attainment of the power of the body; second is the attainment of the power of speech; third is the attainment of the power of the mind; fourth is the attainment of the power of the divine feet; fifth is the attainment of the power of the Path; and sixth is the attainment of the power of wisdom.
Sīhaka Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What constitutes physical strength?
The Buddha said:
"As for his physical strength, it is as firm and powerful as a diamond; it is without flaw or impurity, cannot be burned by fire, cannot be severed by a sword, and no one at all can shake it."
"This is the power of the body.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is the power of speech?
The Buddha said:
"As for the power of speech, there are six kinds of sounds. The sound uttered from the Tathāgata’s mouth can pervade the suns and moons of the trichiliocosm.
This is the power of speech."
“What is the power of the mind?
The Buddha said,
“As for the power of the mind, even if hundreds of thousands of billions of Māras were to come forth, they could not shake a single hair of the Buddha.”
“This is the power of the mind.
“What is the power of the bases of supernormal power?
The Buddha said:

"As for the power of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), by holding up a single toe, one can cause the sun and moon of the trichiliocosm to tremble, yet among the people therein, none shall feel alarm or fear."
"This is the power of the bases of psychic mastery (ṛddhipāda).
What is the power of the path (mārgabala)?
The Buddha said:
"As for the power of the Way: the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the Dharma for all people without any omission or interruption, so that each attains their proper place.
This is called the power of the Way."
“What is the power of wisdom?
The Buddha said:

“The power of wisdom is when all that people know through the mind, know through conduct, know through mindfulness, and know through liberation from mindfulness are gathered together at once; in the space of a finger-snap, one maintains wisdom and fully knows, sees, and realizes everything that can be known, seen, and learned.”
This is the power of wisdom.
Having attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains all-knowledge through these six matters.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The physical courage of this body is immeasurable; there is no one capable of destroying it.
Whether by fire or by sword, it can never be harmed."
Even if all people and their strength were to strike him with staves or revile him, they could not endanger his person nor cause him to fall;
they could not even move a single hair on his body.
The Great-Sounding Śrāvaka Brahmā dwells eternally in fearlessness;
the Dharma he proclaims opens up the three thousandfold world, and none are able to obstruct these words.
The mind is noble and difficult to assail; the nature of all bodhisattvas is spontaneous.
Even if ten billion Māras should seek to disturb them, they could never move their minds.
When his supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) are fully perfected, he can move this heaven and earth;
having accomplished these supernormal powers, he is able to realize the state of the Most Honored One.
If one attains the realization of the Way and Awakening, one is then able to awaken to the state of the Honored Hero;
possessing all the qualities of a Buddha, one then proceeds from this to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Viśākha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Having already perfected all-knowledge, in how many dharmas does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha abide?”
The Buddha said:
"O youth, one who has accomplished all-knowledge,
the Tathāgata abides by means of six dharmas."
What are these six? First, the ten powers of a Buddha;

second, the four fearlessnesses; third, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; fourth, great compassion; fifth, the fact that no one is able to see the crown of a Buddha’s head; and sixth, the possession of the thirty-two marks of a great man.
"These are the six dharmas of abiding.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"The ten powers are the power of the Buddha; The four fearlessnesses have all been transcended."
He has transcended all dharmas; for this reason, he is the leader among men.
Having attained unobstructed compassion, no one can see the crown of the Buddha’s head;
neither gods nor dragons, nor any human beings, can behold it.
Such are the marks of valor, numbering thirty-two in their full extent;
because all these have been perfected, he has become the supreme among men.
Śikhaṇḍin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Having already attained all-knowledge, by means of how many dharmas does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha enter parinirvāṇa?”
The Buddha said,
"O youth, having already attained all-knowledge,
the Tathāgata brings about parinirvāṇa by means of six dharmas."
"What are the six modes of parinirvāṇa?
At that time, O youth!
the Tathāgata leaves behind five aspects of parinirvāṇa."
What are the five? First is the aggregate of ethical discipline;
second is the aggregate of meditative concentration; third is the aggregate of wisdom; fourth is the aggregate of liberation; and fifth is the aggregate of the vision and cognition of liberation.
This is why five parts remain undestroyed out of compassion for all people;
at the time of his parinirvāṇa, O youth!
The Tathāgata, out of compassion for all people, praises and extols the merits of the bhikṣu-saṃgha through countless means, so as to cause people to practice giving.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, O youth,
the Tathāgata will cause his bodily remains to be dispersed like mustard seeds out of compassion for all people.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, O youth!
The Tathāgata has taught the Bodhisattvas that the reason I seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path is solely out of compassion for all people.
At the time of my parinirvāṇa, O youth!
For the sake of the people of the ten directions, the Tathāgata has taught the twelve divisions of the sūtras, so that all people may each attain their proper place.

What are these twelve? First, the Sūtra; second, the Vyākaraṇa (Explanatory Sūtra); third, the Geya (Chanted Sūtra); fourth, the Geya-vibhaṅga (Analytical Chanted Sūtra); fifth, the Udāna (Inspired Utterance); sixth, the Avadāna (Parable); seventh, the Itivṛttaka (Thus-spoken Sūtra); eighth, the Jātaka (Birth Story); ninth, the Vaipulya (Extensive Sūtra); tenth, the Adbhuta-dharma (Marvelous Dharma Sūtra); eleventh, the Upadeśa (Instructional Sūtra); and twelfth, the Kṣudraka (Miscellaneous Sūtra).
These constitute the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Out of compassion and protection for all people, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata extensively expounded the four refuges.
What are these four?
First, to grasp only the essential meaning and not the consciousness;
second, to grasp only the Dharma and not the consciousness;
third, to grasp only wisdom and not the physical form.
Fourth, one takes up only the truth and not the words.
These are the four refuges.
Having attained all-knowledge, O youth!
"The Tathāgata brings about parinirvāṇa by means of these six dharmas.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, He manifested peace and security for all beings."
For the sake of the ten directions, he leaves behind five portions, out of compassion for all humans and non-humans.
He causes his relics to remain in the world as fragments of bone for all beings—
be they as small as mustard seeds or fine grains— and those who obtain them will not fail to revere them.
Those who make offerings therein—whether human or non-human—enjoy boundless bliss;
whether in the heavens or among humans, in whatever place they are born, they shall have no toil or suffering.
Just as when they see me making offerings, so too regarding my parinirvāṇa and my relics—
those whose minds are pure find no difference between these two things.
The Buddha entrusted the community of bhikṣus:
"In that which is most noble and unsurpassed, give great gifts therein; receive the merit of both gods and humans."
The twelve divisions of the sūtras and precepts are preserved; the Buddha abides here throughout the ten directions.
These are what all bodhisattvas ought to practice; now, through repeated cultivation, they give rise to a wholesome mind.
The ten stages (*bhūmi*), the three baskets (*piṭaka*) of scripture, and the *Pramudita-prabhāsa-pāramitā*—all are contained herein.
Compassionate toward all humans and non-humans, he manifested his appearance for future generations.
He then extensively expounded the four refuges; though all dharmas are without support, out of compassion for the mundane world he preached this sutra. At that moment, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the youth Sikhamati spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"I too shall likewise take up the Buddha’s [teaching]. How excellent!
This unsurpassed, swift wisdom—what person, having heard this Dharma, would not give rise to the aspiration for Bodhisattvahood?"
Now these five hundred disciples have all come to this place;
I shall cause them all to resolve their minds, and therefore I exhort them toward the practice of a bodhisattva.
It is like a planter of trees: from moisture a sprout is born, and through moisture it grows large;
then there are the trunk and the joints, followed by branches and leaves;
and from those branches and leaves, flowers are obtained.
Because there are flowers, there are fruits; yet after this, they arise once more.
The intention of the Bodhisattva is likewise: from the six dharmas it arises, and because of this intention one is able to have faith; by being able to perform these dharmas, it is born.
This meaning is revealed as the truth in this sutra, spoken by all Buddhas;
next come the branches and the leaves, which subsequently grow forth once again.
Thus, this tree has attained greatness; the Bodhisattva-tree is unsurpassed.
If one wishes to lean upon this tree, it shall bring peace and security to all.
Such a Dharma is a great tree; for this reason, he is the Buddha, who out of compassion for all people, practices the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Sīhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, how many qualities will there be that cannot be attained even by Pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha said:
“Child! After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there will be six meritorious qualities that are not within the reach of pratyekabuddhas who have attained the proper deportment.
What are these six?

First, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, his relics shall receive offerings; devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, manava-rūpin deities, uraga deities, humans, and non-humans will all come to offer worship to the relics, doing so without end.
Second, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, all people shall emerge from the three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Third, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly of disciples shall practice meritorious offerings to the community of bhikṣus.
Fourth, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, the twelve divisions of the scriptures shall spread throughout Jambudvīpa;

fifth, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, in border regions and great kingdoms where the scriptural Dharma is not understood, and in places lacking righteous principles, the teachings of various non-Buddhists shall flourish;

sixth, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if there are those who hear of the Buddha’s conduct, the Buddha’s supernormal powers, the Buddha’s transformations, and the Buddha’s wisdom, they will largely give rise to pure affection and a mind of reverence; by these causes and conditions, they shall attain rebirth among devas or humans and receive blessings.
"These six merits cannot be equaled by any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"By making offerings to the śarīra, one shall become a deva or a human being."
If one makes offerings to the community of bhikṣus,
they will always protect those bhikṣus who abide in and practice the Dharma, enabling them to transcend the three realms.
If one hears this essential teaching, one should act upon it immediately.
If people in borderlands and various kingdoms hear this unsurpassed Dharma,
or if they hear of the Buddha’s virtues, they shall immediately give rise to the bodhicitta.
Śikhaṇḍin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is the unsurpassed, right, and true path the truth?
The Buddha said:
“There are six dharmas that constitute truth. What are the six?
First, the eye being detached from forms is truth;”
“The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are detached from form; this is the truth.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“The six [senses] are not the ear or the voice or the eye; within them, there is absolutely no form.”
Not looking at one another is the truth; those who wish to train should do so in this way.
The ear and nose are not connected [to one another]; as for this body, speech, and mind, do not allow the mind to give rise to these things. To have no mental constructions is the truth.
The absence of conceptualization is the truth; one should remain far removed from attachment to all forms.
That which is entirely unconditioned is what is called the right truth.
At that time, Sihakāma spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"How wonderful, how excellent is the Dharma of non-thought! Who, upon hearing it, would not aspire to it with joy?"
"May all fears be transcended and liberated, and may there be no attachment to sensual desires.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses for the youth Sikhaṇḍin:
"If one offers no homage to the Buddhas, And shows no reverence toward the True Dharma,"
They do not associate with the Saṃgha, and upon hearing this teaching, they feel no joy.
If there are those who lack faith, whose morality is extremely narrow and inferior,
and who are timid and lacking in diligence, then for them this Dharma is unsuitable.
Abounding in anger and obscured by violence, their wills are deluded and they lack discernment;
being fickle by nature and devoid of wisdom or reflection—such as these, he does not delight in.
If the sons of Māra and the messengers of Māra, as well as those of external paths with false views,
remain firmly established in doubt within the net, they will not believe or accept these words upon hearing them.
Śikhaṇḍin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These people are not vessels for the Dharma; I shall make them vessels for the Dharma.
I only pray that the Buddha will grant me a prediction of my future enlightenment!"
He then spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"Just as one with broken vessels cannot uphold the Great Dharma,
because of this fault of being inferior to others, I shall act for them as a vessel of the Dharma."
I only pray that the Buddha grant me his prediction; now my sincere resolve has arisen from within.
I shall draw near to spiritual friends and seek bodhisattvas who share my aspiration.
I cause those who are poor to become wealthy; I teach those who lack faith so that they may believe;
I cause those who are corrupt and evil to uphold the precepts; for the sake of all beings, I provide protection.
He constantly preaches the purity of forbearance, Guiding others to repent their transgressions;
Through the Samantaprabhā-pāramitā, All wriggling creatures are delivered and liberated.
Teaching people through the dharma of emptiness, Causing all to be liberated from birth and death,
Bestowing upon bodhisattvas the resolve for joy— This is what should be practiced within the Dharma.
The distribution of the relics shall be universal, Causing all sentient beings to attain peace and stability;
The sūtras and precepts shall be left throughout the ten directions, Causing all to constantly practice and follow them.
The Buddha said to the youth Sīhaka:
“All the Buddhas of the past have already conferred upon you the prediction of enlightenment; I, too, shall now likewise confer upon you the prediction.”
"All the Buddhas currently turning the wheel of Dharma in incalculable lands throughout the present have likewise bestowed upon you this prediction of enlightenment.

When the youth Sīhamaitha heard from the Buddha that he had been granted this prediction, he was filled with great joy. He immediately ascended into the air to a height of one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground, descended from above, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, paying homage to the Buddha.
At that time, the five hundred disciples, having witnessed this great transformation, spoke a verse before the Buddha:
“If you would deign to show us compassion through your teaching, we pray only that the Buddha grant us a prediction of our future destiny.
In the future age of the five corruptions and evil, we, as a group, shall uphold the Dharma.”
If they repeatedly admonish and revile me, or if wicked people strike me with whips and staves—
at such times, when there are such persons in the world, I shall teach them to repent and reproach themselves.
At that time, O World-Honored One, we and all others shall endure every suffering and affliction;
for the sake of all humans and non-humans, please grant us this essential resolution.
We are all of us with bodies worn out; we do not covet or begrudge our life-span.
We only wish to delight in solitude and have no longing for offerings.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses for the five hundred disciples:
"These five hundred disciples, who have now all come here,
in a future age, shall all give rise to the bodhisattva mind."
One must still undergo further toil and hardship, and one's lifespan shall be short;
yet at that time, wherever one may be, one will behold offerings beyond measure.
When I first resolved to become a Bodhisattva, I too endured hardships and toil in every lifetime;
you should train yourselves in this same way, and you shall likewise attain the status of a king among men.
The Dharma is fundamentally empty and devoid of self; out of compassion for all, I have repeatedly taught this.
At that time, in that world, I manifested my form for your sake.
All the bodhisattvas were filled with joy and praised him, saying: "The Buddha is eternally present;
for the sake of all, he brings peace and security, manifesting to people the physical form of a Buddha."
Throughout all lands and the ten directions, the present Dharma Kings—
all Buddhas, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, have emitted great rays of light.
The Great Being Ajita Maitreya now resides in the fourth heaven;
he repeatedly exhorts and gladdens all bodhisattvas, and also encourages them by revealing the profound Dharma.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was practicing his conduct, many people all resolved their minds [to follow him].
Yet, as there were residual karmic calamities from past lives, those whose minds were distracted should exhaust their remaining offenses.
The aspirations of his will are insatiable, and he can never satisfy himself;
finding no pleasure in other matters, he constantly seeks the practices of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"Disciples, do not grieve; though this diligent practice cannot last long, after his life in this world has ended, he shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven above."
May I aspire to be born in the land of peace and security, before the Dharma King of infinite life;
within the realm of the Wondrous Medicine King, the place where the Buddha Without Anger provides instruction.
May I always aspire to be born there; when my life in this world has ended, may I immediately attain supernormal powers there and make offerings before all the Buddhas.

By practicing these six dharmas, one attains self-perfection; now, at this time of the Buddha, all receive the prediction of enlightenment, as they are all delivered from the three evil realms and have distanced themselves from the eight difficult conditions.
Having torn asunder all false paths and the great net, he has escaped and gone forth;
unattached and with no further causal conditions, the Pratyekabuddha completely surpasses them all therein.

At that time, when the five hundred disciples heard the Buddha bestow upon them the prediction of their future enlightenment, they were all filled with great joy. They immediately ascended into the air to a height of twenty *zhang* above the ground, then descended from above, prostrated before the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"How may we, Śāriputra and the others, receive our investiture?"

At that time, the Buddha smiled; from his mouth issued rays of light of countless colors, each distinct from the others. The light illuminated countless Buddha-lands, then returned to circle his body three times before vanishing into the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and, bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what cause and condition does the Buddha smile?"
"Since you have smiled, there must be a reason.
At that time, the Buddha spoke this verse for Ānanda:
"Śāriputra stands at the head; Among my disciples, he is the foremost teacher."
They shall all together share a single kalpa, becoming honored heroes among humanity.
During this virtuous and auspicious kalpa, yet in the future age of the five corruptions and evil world,
they shall completely exhaust their karmic retributions therein, and thereby attain supernormal powers.
Thereafter, having perfected his supernormal powers, he flew to billions of buddha-fields;
having made offerings there, he attained Buddhahood, and that Buddha was named Padmottara.
At that time, the five hundred disciples praised the Buddha before him, speaking in verse:
"Now the Buddha speaks of us, declaring that we shall receive our investiture as Buddhas;
he teaches all to perform meritorious deeds, so that innumerable thoughts may not arise."
At that time, I, the Dharma King, shall dwell in Jambudvīpa;
as a Bodhisattva, I will extensively preach the Sūtra of the Way-tree for the sake of all beings.
If anyone, upon hearing this sutra and being questioned about it, immediately gives rise to the aspiration for bodhi, we all exhort the Buddha:
"May the Honored Hero grant us his prediction."
The Buddha of the present is the father of all; He constantly pities humans and non-humans alike.
Out of love for his children, he bestows compassion; The Great Honored One shall now explain this in detail.
At that time, regarding this sutra, they shall thereafter give rise to reverence;
immediately conceiving the aspiration for bodhi, they shall inquire into its meaning for the sake of others.
May the Great Honored Hero explain in full: what virtues does the bodhicitta possess?
If a wise person hears this Dharma, they shall immediately give rise to the bodhicitta.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses for the five hundred disciples:
"If there are those who hear this and believe, I, the Bodhisattva, the Unsurpassed Honored One, Grant them all the prediction of enlightenment; They shall all become Kings among Men."
With a great and courageous resolve as he had wished, he set out directly as a bodhisattva;
his intention being exceedingly pure, he immediately attained birth in a state of pure reality.
Emerging from desire for form and transcending the triple world, one immediately gives rise to the bodhicitta;
by maintaining this mind and performing meritorious deeds, one swiftly attains liberation beyond the triple world.
All actions performed by all people are attached within the three realms;
if one’s mind is without attachment, such a Bodhisattva is unsurpassed.

If a bodhisattva gives rise to the intention for this sutra, acting as a tree of the Way for all beings, they will possess merit and provide instruction; by upholding this sutra, they are able to manifest it.
The deeds of the Bodhisattvas have been fully explained, and all that ought to be taught has been set forth in their entirety;
yet other dharmas are beyond counting, for those dharmas are so subtle they cannot be described.
Fully endowed with immeasurable wisdom, By means of this, he has attained Buddhahood;
Out of compassion for all people, He constantly cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld and practiced?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Way under the Tree'; you should recite and uphold it!
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason is it called the 'Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Tree of Enlightenment'?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"It is like planting a tree: first a sprout gradually emerges, and later the trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit are produced."

Thus it is, Ānanda! In this sutra, a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind upon awakening immediately attains joy; from that joy, body and mind find rest. They become fully endowed with the practice of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), manifesting transformative wisdom and brilliant virtue. They then attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and become fully endowed with all-encompassing wisdom. They turn the wheel of Dharma and continue until their final nirvana, after which they distribute their relics so that they may abide for successive generations through the application of the Dharma.
"Therefore, Ānanda, this is called the 'Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Way-Tree.

When the Buddha had finished speaking, the youth Sīhaka with his five hundred disciples, the assembly of bhikṣus, as well as devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, and kumbhāṇḍas, having heard this sūtra, were all greatly rejoiced. They came forward, prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground in homage to the Buddha, and then departed."
The Sutra of the Questions of Śrīgupta (Śrīguptaparipṛcchā-sūtra)
